You recognise and use the three registers of French (informal, standard, formal) and switch between them depending on the situation.
Have you seen? It is quite remarkable. (formal)
Haven’t got time, I’ve got to work. (informal)
I do not have the necessary time at my disposal. (formal)
Recognise the most common informal vocabulary (bosser, boulot, bagnole, fric, mec, kiffer).
Understand a few verlan words (meuf, ouf, relou, chelou, vénère).
Recognise the grammatical features of informal French (dropping “ne”, “t’as”, “y a”, “on”).
Use the vocabulary and constructions of formal French (inversion, demeurer, néanmoins).
Choose the right register for the situation (friends, school, official letter, exam).
Monday, 15 June 2036, evening, in Julien’s kitchen. Sami, 18, has written a slam about the waltz for the Fête de la musique. Inès is reading it, and Julien is listening.
So? Did you like it or not? Be honest, I’ve been working on it all week.
It’s amazing, Sami. But there are words nobody will understand except us. “Relou”, “chelou”, “vénère”…
Well, that’s on purpose. That’s how we talk in La Duchère. I’m not gonna write like a teacher.
You’re right. A slam isn’t a letter to the prefecture. The informal register is your colour.
OK. But at the end you make Odile speak. Do you really think she’d have said “the chick across the way”?
(he laughs) No, you’re right. She’d have said: “Young lady, would you be so kind as to answer me?”
Not quite. Odile spoke plain, simple, everyday French. She’d have said: “If you can hear me, answer me.”
So there’s your idea: each character speaks in their own register. You in verlan, Odile in everyday French…
…and the 1978 sailor in Marseille slang! Awesome. But someone has to speak formally, otherwise it’s not complete.
The prefect, maybe? “Ladies and gentlemen, it is nevertheless fitting to remain silent for the duration of eight bars.”
(she bursts out laughing) Perfect! Nobody talks like that. That’s exactly why it works.
OK, I’ll rework everything tonight. But I’m keeping “ouf”. That’s not negotiable.
Keep it. Odile would have loved that word. She’d have asked what it meant, then used it every day.
(“il convient de” = it is fitting to)
“Ta”, “ya”: in informal speech, sounds contract and “il” disappears.
The same idea can be said in three ways. You choose the register according to the situation, not according to how “well” you speak:
Je ne dispose pas des fonds nécessaires.
Il exerce au sein d’une société.
In the DELF B2 exam, use the standard-to-formal register. You only need to UNDERSTAND the informal register (in the audio documents).
Informal words are everywhere in films, songs and podcasts. Don’t use them in an official letter or a job interview.
Verlan reverses the syllables of a word (“l’envers” → “verlan”). It was born in the suburbs and then spread to the language of young people all over France:
Don’t use verlan to “sound” natural: a foreigner who gets it wrong sounds odd. Learn it so you can understand it.
Y a du monde. Faut partir.
Il y a du monde. Il faut partir.
Tu as faim ? Je suis là.
Dropping “ne” is normal in all French people’s everyday speech, even teachers’. In writing, however, it must be kept.
The formal register is recognisable by inversion, rare vocabulary and long constructions:
Would you be so kind as to answer me? (inversion + rare vocabulary)
It is fitting to remain silent. (il convient de, demeurer)
I am going to Paris tomorrow. (se rendre = aller)
Nevertheless, I would like to meet you. (néanmoins, souhaiter)
Useful pairs: aller → se rendre; habiter → demeurer; vouloir → souhaiter; mais → néanmoins / toutefois; commencer → débuter; finir → achever.
Which is the STANDARD version of “J’ai pas de fric.”?
Which sentence is in the FORMAL register?
“Il bosse dans une boîte” in the standard register:
Il travaille dans une boîte en carton.
I’m going to Paris tomorrow. (formal, se rendre)
It is fitting to remain silent.
Pour quelle occasion Sami a-t-il écrit un slam ?
C’est comme ça qu’on parle à La Duchère
Il ne connaît pas d’autres mots
Quel mot Sami refuse-t-il de changer ?
Nevertheless, I would like to meet you.

Sami was eighteen and had never shown anyone what he wrote. He had been filling notebooks since the age of twelve, in the evenings, in his room on the eleventh floor of a tower block in La Duchère, while his mother slept after her cleaning shifts. Sentences, rhymes, scraps of conversations overheard on the bus. He hid the notebooks under his mattress, the way other people hide money or love letters.

The first notebook, a blue spiral one, dated from the year his father left. Sami was twelve. He never talked about it. That evening he had written just one sentence, which he had never shown anyone: “When someone leaves, the words stay.” After that he had carried on. One notebook a year, then two, then four. He now had twenty-three, piled under the mattress, so that his bed had become lopsided.

Everyone in Lyon knew Sami for something else. He was the boy with the flute, the one who had played the waltz for the first time in the school playground years before, the one who had taught Inès’s mother the flute, the one who had played in the Thursday orchestra from the start. He was in his final year at the Croix-Rousse lycée, he got good marks, and he spoke little. Nobody knew he wrote.

Nobody except Inès. She had found the notebooks by chance one afternoon in March, looking for a pen in his bag. She had read three pages before he noticed. He had gone bright red and snatched the notebook out of her hands. Inès hadn’t apologised. She had said she had read hundreds of texts for her eloquence contests, and his were among the best. Then she had said he had to perform them in public.

Sami had refused. He had said his texts were written the way people talk in La Duchère, with words city-centre people wouldn’t understand. Verlan, slang, sentences without “ne”, Arabic words his mother used. He had said that if he read that in public, people would laugh at him. Or worse: they would find him exotic. Inès had replied that she had won a national contest with a text about culture. She knew what she was talking about.

Yanis, his best friend since nursery school, had known nothing about the notebooks until April. When Inès told him, he was offended. He said best friends should tell each other everything. Sami replied that best friends should above all know how to keep quiet. Yanis thought about it, then said it was a very good sentence and he should write it down somewhere. Sami showed him he already had. In notebook number nine.

It was Théo who found the solution. For the Fête de la musique, on Saturday 21 June, the Thursday orchestra was to play on a big stage on the Place des Terreaux, on the very spot where the first filmed silence had taken place three years earlier. Théo was looking for something new to go with the waltz. Inès had told him about the notebooks. Théo had asked Sami whether he could write a slam about the waltz. Just one. For the Fête de la musique.

It took Sami three weeks to say yes, and another three to write the text. He wrote it in one go, one night in May, then rewrote it twenty times. It was called “Eight Bars”. It told the story of the waltz, from the Dakar quay to the Bucharest piano, but told by a boy from La Duchère who had first heard it in a school playground without knowing where it came from.

To find the sailor’s words, Sami had called Yves Le Goff in Brittany. The old sailor was ninety-two, with his memory intact. For an hour on the phone he recited all the port slang he knew: the words for the wind, the sea, the captain, the money you didn’t have. Some were so crude that Sami had to look them up in a specialist dictionary. Yves laughed, saying he couldn’t say more in front of his nurse.

The first person to hear the whole text was Rose-Hélène. Sami chose her because she was eight and never lied. He recited it to her in the courtyard of the rue d’Austerlitz building, sitting on a bench, in a low voice. Rose-Hélène listened to the end without moving. Then she said she hadn’t understood half the words, but she had understood everything anyway. Sami said it was the nicest compliment anyone had ever paid him.

Rose-Hélène added one remark. In the text, Sami made all the characters talk the way he did, in verlan, including Odile and the old sailor. She found that strange. Grandma Odile would never have said “c’est ouf”. Nor would the sailor, probably. She said everyone should speak in their own words, as in real life. Sami looked at her for a long time. Then he took out his notebook and crossed everything out.

On Monday 15 June, Sami brought the new version to Julien’s. Inès was there. They spent the evening in the kitchen discussing each character and their way of speaking. The boy from La Duchère in verlan. Odile in everyday French, simple and warm. The 1978 sailor in Marseille slang, with harbour words. And to finish, an imaginary prefect who spoke such formal French that nobody understood what he meant.

Julien had helped with the prefect. He had great fun writing endless sentences full of “il convient de”, “néanmoins” and imperfect subjunctives. Inès had helped with the Marseille slang, which she had picked up from a great-aunt. Rose-Hélène, listening from the corridor in her pyjamas, had helped with Odile. She knew her expressions by heart, because Isabelle often repeated them: “My little one”, “It’ll be fine”, “Come on, let’s go”.

By midnight the text was finished. Sami read it aloud one last time in the kitchen, in front of Inès, Julien and Ioana, who had come home late from a building site. When he stopped, nobody spoke for a while. Then Ioana said she had learnt French from textbooks, grammars and vocabulary lists, and in ten years she had never heard anyone play with the language like that. She said that if she had had this text when she arrived in Lyon, she would have learnt twice as fast.

Meanwhile, at the other end of the flat, another question of register was stirring up the family. Henri-Ion had come home from school with a new word. A swear word. He had said it at dinner, very proudly, with a perfect accent. Ioana had nearly choked. Julien asked where he had learnt it. Henri-Ion explained it was Malik, a big boy in Year 4, and that it was a word you said when you hurt yourself.

Julien explained to him, very seriously, that there were words for every situation. Words for school, words for friends, words for home, and words you didn’t say at all, even when you hurt yourself. Henri-Ion asked which words you should say when you hurt yourself, then. Julien thought about it. He suggested “ouch”. Henri-Ion found it much less effective. Ioana had to leave the table to laugh in the kitchen.

Over the following days Sami rehearsed everywhere. On the bus, under his breath, so that passengers turned round. On the stairs of the tower block, because the lift was broken. In front of the bathroom mirror, until his mother knocked on the door. Inès coached him as if for an eloquence contest: breathing, pauses, eye contact. She kept telling him that a well-placed silence was worth more than ten rhymes. Sami said that for that, he already had a good teacher. The waltz.

On the day of the Fête de la musique, the Place des Terreaux was packed from six in the evening. It was hot, almost thirty degrees. There were rock bands in the neighbouring streets, a gospel choir outside the Town Hall, an old man playing the accordion on a pavement. And in the middle of the square, the big stage, with the forty musicians of the Thursday orchestra, their music stands and their scores flying away in the wind.

Sami was waiting in the wings, behind the stage, with his notebook, which he no longer looked at. He knew it by heart. He had had a stomach ache since the morning. His mother was there, in the front row, in her party dress, with her neighbours from the tower. It was the first time she had come to hear him. Her name was Leïla. She had been cleaning offices for twenty-five years and had brought up her son alone, on the eleventh floor, without ever complaining.

At nine o’clock the orchestra began the waltz. After the second verse, Théo lowered his baton, and the musicians carried on playing very softly, almost silently. Sami walked on stage. He was wearing a black T-shirt and jeans. He had no microphone in his hand, just a small one clipped to his collar. He walked to the edge of the stage. Three thousand people were watching him. He closed his eyes. Then he began.

First he spoke like a boy from La Duchère. Fast, with clipped words, verlan, rhymes that slammed like doors. He told of a school playground, a rainy afternoon, a teacher making children who couldn’t care less play a waltz. In the audience, the young people recognised their language straight away. They cheered. The older ones frowned. Some didn’t understand one word in three.

Then his voice changed. It became slower, softer, older. It was Odile speaking. An old lady on a landing, with her plants and her watering can, whistling off-key and waiting for someone to answer. She said very simple things, in everyday French: “My little one, it’ll be fine.” “If you can hear me, answer me.” In the audience, Isabelle put her hand to her mouth. It was exactly her mother’s voice.

Then came the sailor, with a Marseille accent you could cut with a knife, dockers’ curses and harbour words nobody had heard for fifty years. The audience laughed. An old man in the front row, originally from Marseille, shouted “Bravo, lad!” Then came the prefect, with his endless sentences, his “il convient de” and his imperfect subjunctives. The whole square burst out laughing. Even the real prefect, invited that evening, laughed.

And then, in the middle of the text, Sami stopped. Dead. So did the orchestra. It was the third verse. Eight bars. Sami stood motionless at the edge of the stage, eyes open this time, facing the three thousand people. And the three thousand people fell silent. The young ones with their verlan, the old men from Marseille, the families, the tourists, the prefect. On the Place des Terreaux, all you could hear was the wind and, in the distance, a rock band that didn’t know.

After the silence, Sami started again. But this time he no longer spoke as a single character. He mixed them all. A sentence in verlan, a sentence from Odile, a sailor’s word, a prefect’s word. The registers answered one another like the voices of the waltz. And at the end, all together, they said the same thing, each in their own words: that the language belonged to nobody, and that everyone had the right to answer it.

The last word of the text was “ouf”. Sami said it very softly, almost in a breath. Then he bowed his head. For two seconds there was no sound at all. Then the square exploded. The young people shouted, the old people applauded, the tourists filmed. In the front row, Leïla was crying without trying to hide it. Her neighbours from the tower held her by the shoulders. Bernard Delorme, forgetting it wasn’t planned, played a fanfare on the trumpet.

In the wings after the concert, everyone wanted to shake Sami’s hand. Young people from his neighbourhood who had never looked at him at school. Strangers. The old man from Marseille, who told him he hadn’t heard those harbour words since his father died. The real prefect, who asked him very seriously whether he really talked like that. Sami answered no, not always. Only on Sundays. It took the prefect three seconds to realise it was a joke.

Léonie Garnier had filmed the whole scene, with Sami’s permission, which she had asked for three times. She put the video online that same night, at midnight. By the next morning it had been watched a hundred thousand times. The day after, a million. After a week, more than four million people had heard Sami say “ouf” at the end of his text. In the comments there were messages in forty languages.

But not everyone was enthusiastic. On Tuesday, a famous columnist on a national radio station devoted five minutes to Sami’s slam. He said it was nice, admittedly, but that it was the symbol of a language in decline. He talked about “the language of the estates”, about “impoverished French”. He said young people shouldn’t be encouraged to talk like that, and that school should rather teach them to speak properly.

Sami listened to the column on the bus on the way to school. He said nothing. That evening he didn’t come to orchestra rehearsal. He didn’t answer Inès’s messages or Julien’s. He switched off his phone. His mother said he had stayed in his room all evening, without eating, with his notebooks. She had heard pages being torn. She had knocked on the door. He hadn’t opened it.

The next day at school, pupils Sami didn’t know stopped him in the corridors. Some repeated his lines, laughing. Others told him the column had made them angry, because it was about them too. A Year 11 girl told him her grandmother, who had come from Portugal in 1970, had been ashamed of her accent for fifty years, and had cried listening to the slam. Sami didn’t answer. He just kept the grandmother’s name in his head.

Inès didn’t switch off her phone. She spent the night writing. Not a slam: an op-ed. She wrote it in the most formal French she knew, the kind she used for her law essays, with imperfect subjunctives, inversions and quotations from Montaigne. She sent it the next morning to a major national daily. The title was: “Letter to a columnist who speaks badly”.

In her op-ed, Inès explained, with icy politeness, that the columnist had confused two things: speaking badly and speaking differently. She pointed out that Molière made his peasants speak in dialect, that Victor Hugo had put thieves’ slang into “Les Misérables”, and that nobody had ever accused those authors of impoverishing the language. She concluded that someone who could speak only one register was, deep down, the poorer of the two.

Before sending it, Inès had shown her op-ed to Mrs Fontaine, her civil law lecturer, a strict woman who marked every paper in green ink. The lecturer had underlined two agreement errors and a misattributed quotation. Then she had written at the bottom of the last page, still in green ink: “Publish it.” Inès kept the marked copy. She said it was the only “yes” in green ink she had ever received.

The op-ed was published on Thursday. It was read almost as much as the video had been watched. Teachers printed it for their pupils. Writers shared it. The columnist didn’t reply. But on Friday morning, a letter arrived at the headquarters of the “Musique en partage” network, addressed to “Monsieur Sami, the young slam poet from La Duchère”. The envelope was thick, cream-coloured, written with a fountain pen. On the back there was a seal: “Académie française”.

Amina, who was opening the network’s mail despite her maternity leave, with Awa asleep against her in the baby carrier, at first thought it was a joke. She called Julien. Julien called Inès. Inès took a bus, then another, then climbed the eleven floors of the tower on foot because the lift was broken, as usual. She knocked on Sami’s door for five minutes. He finally opened it. His eyes were red.

The letter was signed Hortense Valmont, of the Académie française. Sami had never heard the name. Inès had. Hortense Valmont was a linguist, eighty-two years old, a member of the Académie for twenty years, and known as the strictest guardian of the French language. She had written whole books against anglicisms. Inès expected the worst. Sami handed her the letter unopened. He didn’t have the courage.

Inès opened it and read it aloud in the small room on the eleventh floor, sitting on the bed among the torn pages. The letter began badly: the old lady admitted that some words had shocked her. Sami closed his eyes. Then the letter changed tone. Hortense Valmont said she had listened to the slam three times. That she had understood. That she had been born in La Duchère, in 1954, in a building that no longer existed.

At the end of the letter, when Inès read the invitation to the Académie, on Thursday 2 July, quai de Conti, Sami opened his eyes. He asked Inès to read it again. She did. He asked whether it was a joke. Inès said that as far as she knew, the Académie française didn’t make jokes, at least not since 1635. Then Sami laughed. For the first time in three days. Then he began picking up the torn pages, one by one.

The week before leaving, Sami asked Inès how you dressed to go to the Académie française. Inès said she had no idea. Julien offered to lend him a tie. Leïla wanted to buy him a suit. Rose-Hélène said he must come exactly as at the Fête de la musique, in a black T-shirt, because that was the boy the academician had invited, not another one. Everyone fell silent. Sami kept the T-shirt.

The evening the letter arrived, Inès found Sami at the edge of the La Duchère park, on the bench where they used to sit as children, next to the old lime tree Rose-Hélène had been watering for years. They sat for a long time without speaking. Then Sami asked whether she thought he had the right to go to the Académie with his own words. Inès replied that he didn’t just have the right. He had the duty. Because thousands of kids from La Duchère would never go in there, and he would go in for them.

On Thursday 2 July they took the seven o’clock TGV to Paris. Sami, Inès, Leïla, Julien, Rose-Hélène and Yanis, who had insisted on coming as “bodyguard”. Leïla had put on her best dress, the one from the Fête de la musique, and was holding on her knees a bag of honey cakes she had made all night for the academician. She kept asking whether it was polite to bring cakes to the Académie française.

Julien said he had no idea, but that nobody had ever refused a honey cake. Rose-Hélène added that Grandma Odile always brought something when she visited anyone, even the doctor. Leïla relaxed a little. Then she told them that at twenty, arriving from Algeria, she had cleaned ministries in Paris at night. She used to walk past the Académie on her way home, at five in the morning. She had never imagined going inside.

The Académie stood on the bank of the Seine, opposite the Louvre, beneath a great gilded dome. Hortense Valmont was waiting for them in the courtyard, leaning on a silver-handled cane. She was a small, thin woman, with white hair in a bun and very bright eyes. She wore an impeccable grey suit. She shook everyone’s hand very ceremoniously. Then she stopped in front of Sami. She looked at him for a long time. She said: “So you’re the lad from La Duchère.”

Sami answered “yes, madame” in a voice he didn’t recognise. Hortense Valmont smiled. Then she said, with a Lyon accent she obviously hadn’t used for sixty years: “Don’t worry, I’m not gonna eat you.” Inès nearly fell over. Rose-Hélène burst out laughing. Leïla held out her honey cakes. The academician took one at once, tasted it and declared they were the best cakes anyone had brought her since her election.

Walking across the courtyard, Hortense Valmont told Sami about her childhood. She had grown up on the seventh floor of a long block in La Duchère, demolished long ago. Her mother said “bagnole”, “boulot”, “pognon”. At school a teacher had taught her to say “voiture”, “travail”, “argent”, and for years she had been ashamed of the way her mother spoke. She said that shame was the only thing she truly regretted in her life.

She showed them round the Académie herself, slowly, leaning on her cane. The great assembly hall beneath the dome, with its wooden benches and numbered armchairs. The library, where four-hundred-year-old books slept. The Dictionary room, where the academicians had met every Thursday afternoon for centuries to discuss the words of the French language, one by one. They had reached the letter S, she said. They had been working on it since 1986.

Rose-Hélène did the sum out loud. She said that at that speed they would never get to the O of “ouf”. Hortense Valmont laughed. She said that in any case “ouf” began with an O, and they had passed it long ago without including it. Then she added, more quietly, that the language always moved faster than the dictionary. That was precisely why it was alive.

At three o’clock they entered the Dictionary room. About twenty academicians were sitting round a long table covered with papers, old dictionaries and coffee cups. There were writers, a former minister, a cardinal, a physicist, a historian, a film director. Most were over seventy. When Sami walked in, in a black T-shirt and jeans, notebook in hand, twenty pairs of eyes looked at him over twenty pairs of glasses.

Hortense Valmont introduced him in a few words, in perfectly formal French. She said she had invited this young man to remind them of something academicians sometimes forgot: that the French language was not a museum, but a house where millions of people lived. Then she sat down and said: “Monsieur, we are listening.” Silence fell. An old writer at the end of the table had already fallen asleep.

Sami began. Without the orchestra this time. Without a microphone. Just his voice, in that silent room where words had been discussed for four centuries. He made the boy from La Duchère speak, and the cardinal raised an eyebrow. He made Odile speak, and the historian took off her glasses. He made the Marseille sailor speak, and the former minister laughed in spite of himself. Then he made the prefect speak, and the whole table burst out laughing, recognising themselves.

Then came the silence. Sami stopped in the middle of a sentence. Eight bars. There was no orchestra to mark them, but he counted them in his head. The academicians didn’t know they were supposed to be silent. They fell silent anyway, intrigued, the way you fall silent before someone about to say something important. And at the end of the table, the old sleeping writer woke up. At exactly that moment. He looked around, surprised by the silence.

On the fifth bar, Hortense Valmont did something no academician had ever done in that room. She whistled. Three notes. Off-key, of course. The first three notes of the waltz. The academicians stared at her, astonished. Then, from the other end of the table, the old writer who had just woken up whistled the next three notes. He didn’t know why. He said later it had come to him by itself, like a childhood memory.

Sami finished his text. When he said the last word, “ouf”, very softly, the academicians didn’t applaud at once. They didn’t know whether you were allowed to applaud in the Dictionary room. It was the cardinal who started. Then the physicist. Then all the others. They stood up one after another, leaning on their canes, on the table, on their neighbour’s arm. Leïla, at the back of the room, could no longer see anything through her tears.

The cardinal came up to Sami after the applause. He was a very tall, very thin man with enormous hands. He asked him quietly what “vénère” meant. Sami explained. The cardinal thought about it, then said he knew a Latin word that meant almost the same thing, and that from now on he would use it thinking of him. The old writer who had whistled asked Sami to send him the text. He wanted to learn it by heart. At ninety.

After the session, Hortense Valmont took Sami to her office, a small room filled with books up to the ceiling. She took from a shelf an old leather-bound dictionary covered with pencil notes. It was her own copy, the one she had used for forty years. She opened it at the letter O. In the margin, between “oudiste” and “ouest”, she wrote in pencil, in her fine slanting hand: “ouf: fou, backwards. See Sami, La Duchère, 2036.”

Then she gave him the dictionary. Sami refused. He said it was too precious. Hortense Valmont said that at eighty-two you no longer kept precious things. You gave them to those who would do something with them. She added that she demanded just one thing in return: that he keep writing. In every register. Verlan, formal French and everything in between. She said the language needed people who knew how to go from one door to another.

On the quai de Conti, as they left, Leïla stopped in front of the great door. She looked at the gilded dome for a long time in silence. Then she said something to her son in Arabic, which he never wanted to translate for anyone. Inès only noticed that Sami had taken his mother’s hand. They walked like that to the Pont des Arts, mother and son, without a word, the old dictionary clutched under his arm.

On the train home, Rose-Hélène fell asleep on Yanis’s shoulder. Julien was reading. Inès watched the fields go by. Sami was writing. He hadn’t taken out his old notebook, the one with the torn pages. He was writing on the flyleaf of the dictionary, in pencil, like Hortense. Inès glanced at it. It was a new text. It was neither in verlan nor in formal French. It was written in both at once. The title was: “The house of words”.

Back in Lyon, Sami wrote Hortense Valmont a thank-you letter. He rewrote it seven times. The first version was in verlan, to make her laugh. The second in formal French, to do her honour. The next five tried to find a balance. In the end he sent a three-line letter in plain everyday French, the way Odile would have written it: “Madame, thank you. I’m still writing. If you can hear me, answer me.” Hortense replied by return of post. With three musical notes.

A few days later the baccalauréat results were published. Sami had obtained a “très bien” distinction. He enrolled in modern literature at the University of Lyon. The radio columnist never mentioned the Académie. But when the new term began in September, he devoted an entire column to the word “ouf”, its history and origin. He concluded by saying that it was, after all, rather a pretty word. Inès said that was his way of answering.

Leïla framed the letter from the Académie and hung it in the hall of the flat, above the shoe cabinet, where all the neighbours could see it as they went by. She told the story to anyone who came up to the eleventh floor, including the lift repairman, who came every week. She said “the Académie” with great respect, and “ouf” with great pride. Sami had given up asking her to take the frame down.

When school started again, Rose-Hélène’s teacher in Year 5 asked each pupil to bring a word they loved. Rose-Hélène brought “ouf”. The teacher frowned and asked whether it was really a French word. Rose-Hélène replied that it appeared in an academician’s dictionary, in pencil, between “oudiste” and “ouest”. She added that if the teacher didn’t believe her, she could write to the Académie. The teacher accepted the word. She didn’t write to the Académie.

One July evening, back in La Duchère, Sami went out onto the eleventh-floor balcony. Opposite, in the other tower blocks, the windows were open because of the heat. You could hear televisions, arguments, laughter, children, Arabic music, rap, a radio in Portuguese. Sami whistled three notes, very loudly, into the night. For a moment, nothing. Then, from a balcony somewhere, someone answered. Then another. In all the languages of the neighbourhood.

The letter sent to Sami by Hortense Valmont, a member of the Académie française, after she saw his slam. It is written in the formal register. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Sir, allow an old lady whom you do not know in the least to address these few lines to you. I have had occasion to watch your slam, entitled “Eight Bars”, and I could not conceal my emotion from you.

I confess: on first hearing, some of your words shocked me. “Ouf”, “relou”, “vénère” do not appear at all in the dictionary I have been helping to compile for twenty years. I thought I saw in them a language mistreated.

Nevertheless, I listened to it again. Then a third time. And I understood that you were not mistreating the language at all: you were bringing it to life. Each character in it speaks according to their station and their heart, as in Molière.

I must make you a confession. I was born in 1954 in La Duchère, in a building that no longer exists. My father was a bricklayer. My mother said “bagnole” and “boulot”. I learnt formal French at school, the way one learns a foreign language.

For sixty years I believed I had to choose between my mother’s language and that of the Académie. Your slam has shown me the opposite. One can remain faithful to one’s neighbourhood while inhabiting the language in its entirety.

I would therefore have the honour of inviting you to the Académie, quai de Conti, on Thursday 2 July. I should like you to perform your text there. I do not promise that my colleagues will understand everything. They nonetheless need it greatly. — Hortense Valmont, of the Académie française
(“tout en” = while; “tout entière” = in its entirety)
